blocks.text: Writing an MCP server that works on your laptop is the easy part.

The harder question, the one that decides whether real users can actually depend on it, is how you get that server running somewhere durable, reachable, and able to survive a restart, a traffic spike, or a bad deploy.

There is no single right answer here, a weekend project and a company wide internal tool have very different needs, and the goal of this lesson is to give you a clear map of the main deployment shapes an MCP server can take, along with the tradeoffs that should actually drive your choice.
1. Why Deployment Strategy Matters

An MCP server is, underneath all its protocol machinery, an ordinary long running program. The deployment strategy you pick decides how that program is started, how it is kept running, how it is updated, and what happens when it crashes. Get this wrong and you end up with a server that works great in a demo and then falls over the first time real traffic, a restart, or a bad deploy hits it.

Deployment strategy also shapes almost everything downstream of it, how you scale, how you monitor, how you roll back a bad release, even how you think about cost. That is why this topic opens the Production MCP module, every later lesson on scaling, load balancing, and observability assumes you have already picked one of the shapes described here.

blocks.title: This is a menu, not a ranking
blocks.content: Single process, containerized, and serverless are not tiers of sophistication where one is strictly better than the others. Each is the right answer for a different combination of traffic pattern, team size, and operational appetite.

blocks.text: It also helps to separate two questions that get conflated a lot in practice, how the code is packaged, and where that package actually runs. A container is just a packaging format, it can still be deployed as a single always on replica, as a fleet of replicas behind a load balancer, or even invoked in a serverless style by some platforms. Keeping these two questions distinct makes the rest of this lesson much easier to reason about.
2. Single Process Deployment

blocks.alt: MCP server code branches into single process, container, and serverless deployment paths

blocks.text: The simplest possible deployment is running your MCP server as a single long lived process on a single machine, whether that machine is a laptop, an internal server, or a small cloud instance. There is no orchestration layer, no container runtime, no scaling logic, just your server binary or script started once and left running.

code.content:
# a minimal systemd unit for a single-process deployment
[Unit]
Description=weather-mcp-server
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/weather-mcp/server.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
User=mcp

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

blocks.text: This shape is common for stdio based servers used by a single developer tool, a code editor spawning a local process, or an internal script only ever used by one team. It is also a perfectly reasonable starting point for an HTTP server with modest, predictable traffic, provided you pair it with a process supervisor like systemd or supervisord so a crash results in an automatic restart rather than silent downtime.
3. Containerized Deployment

Packaging an MCP server as a container gives you a consistent, reproducible unit that runs the same way on your laptop, in a staging environment, and in production. The container bundles the interpreter, dependencies, and your code together, so "it works on my machine" stops being a meaningful excuse, the image either runs correctly or it does not.

code.content:
docker build -t weather-mcp-server:1.4.0 .
docker run -d --name weather-mcp \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e API_KEY="$WEATHER_API_KEY" \
  weather-mcp-server:1.4.0

blocks.text: Containers also open the door to orchestration, a container that can run once can usually be scheduled across many machines, restarted automatically on failure, and scaled to several replicas, all without changing a line of application code. The Dockerizing MCP Servers lesson right after this one walks through building that image in detail.
4. Serverless Deployment

A serverless deployment hands the entire question of "where does this process live" to a cloud platform. You upload a handler function, the platform starts an instance of it on demand when a request arrives, runs it, and shuts it back down when it is idle. You never manage a server, a container host, or a restart policy directly.

This model fits bursty, unpredictable traffic extremely well, you pay only for the milliseconds your handler actually runs, and you never provision capacity for a peak that might not arrive. It fits stdio based servers poorly, since stdio assumes one long lived process holding open a pipe to a single client for its entire session, which is exactly the opposite of what a platform that spins instances up and down on demand wants to do.
5. Comparing the Three Models

Laid side by side, the three approaches trade off operational simplicity, scaling behavior, and cost in fairly predictable ways. None of them is free of downsides, the table below is meant to make the tradeoffs explicit rather than to declare a winner.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model","Operational effort","Scaling","Cold starts","Best fit"],"rows":[["Single process","Low","Manual, vertical only","None","Internal tools, low traffic, stdio clients"],["Containerized","Medium","Horizontal, orchestrated","Rare, on new replica start","Team or company wide HTTP servers"],["Serverless","Low to medium","Automatic, near instant","Common on cold instances","Bursty or unpredictable HTTP traffic"]]}

blocks.text: It is worth reading this table as a starting point for a conversation, not a lookup table with one correct row per project. Plenty of real systems mix models across different tools or environments, a pattern covered later in this lesson under hybrid deployment patterns.
6. stdio Transport and Deployment Constraints

blocks.alt: stdio transport constraints are compared against HTTP transport flexibility

blocks.text: A server built around stdio transport is, by design, spawned as a child process of exactly one client and communicates over that client's standard input and output.
This tightly couples the server's lifetime to the client that launched it, which makes single process deployment the natural, almost the only, fit.
There is no meaningful way to run a stdio server behind a load balancer or spin up five replicas of it, since there is no shared network endpoint for a load balancer to sit in front of.

items: A stdio server is started fresh for every client session, so there is nothing persistent to deploy in the traditional sense.
Containerizing a stdio server is still useful for dependency isolation, but the container is launched per session, not left running as a shared service.
Serverless platforms built around HTTP invocation generally cannot host a stdio server at all, since there is no pipe to spawn it over.

blocks.text: 7. HTTP Transport and Deployment Flexibility

An MCP server exposed over HTTP is a normal network service, and that single fact is what unlocks every deployment model discussed in this lesson. An HTTP server can sit behind a load balancer with many identical replicas, it can be packaged as a container and scheduled by an orchestrator, or it can be wrapped as a serverless handler invoked per request.

This is one of the clearest practical reasons teams choose HTTP transport for anything beyond a single developer local tool, not because HTTP is inherently better, but because it is the transport that every later lesson in this module, load balancing, horizontal scaling, high availability, actually assumes.
8. Choosing Based on Team Size and Traffic

A useful first filter is simply asking who depends on this server and how much traffic it realistically sees. A server used by three engineers on an internal tool rarely justifies a Kubernetes cluster, a single well supervised process, or a small container, is plenty. A server backing a customer facing product with unpredictable spikes is exactly where containerized or serverless deployment starts paying for itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Reasonable starting point"],"rows":[["One internal team, steady low traffic","Single process with a supervisor"],["Multiple teams, predictable moderate traffic","Containerized, small fixed replica count"],["Public facing, spiky or unpredictable traffic","Serverless, or containerized with autoscaling"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Choosing Based on Latency Requirements

If your server backs an interactive tool where a user is waiting on a response, cold start latency becomes a first class concern. Serverless platforms are excellent at scaling to zero when idle, but that same behavior means the very first request after a quiet period pays the cost of starting a fresh instance, loading dependencies, and warming any caches, often adding hundreds of milliseconds or more.

A containerized deployment with a small always on replica count avoids this entirely, at the cost of paying for capacity even while it sits idle. There is no universally correct tradeoff here, only a question of whether your users would notice, and tolerate, an occasional slow first request.

blocks.title: Measure before you assume
blocks.content: Do not guess at cold start impact, measure it. Deploy a small canary on the serverless platform you are considering, send it a request after a realistic idle period, and record the actual latency before deciding it is or is not acceptable for your users.

blocks.text: 10. Cold Starts and Serverless Tradeoffs

blocks.alt: A cold start delays the first request after a serverless function has been idle

blocks.text: Cold starts deserve a closer look since they are the single biggest surprise teams run into after moving an MCP server to a serverless platform. The delay comes from several stacked costs, provisioning a fresh execution environment, loading your runtime and dependencies, and running any module level initialization your server does before it can answer its first request.

code.content:
# keep module-level init minimal to reduce cold start time
import os

# heavy imports and client construction happen once per cold start,
# so keep this list as small as the server can get away with
import httpx

_client = None

def get_client():
    global _client
    if _client is None:
        _client = httpx.Client(timeout=5.0)
    return _client

blocks.text: Many platforms offer a "provisioned concurrency" or "warm instance" option that keeps a minimum number of instances running at all times specifically to sidestep this, effectively turning part of your serverless deployment back into an always on one, at a matching part of the cost.
11. State and Deployment Model

blocks.alt: A stateless design fits every deployment model while stateful design does not

blocks.text: How much state your server keeps in memory between requests strongly influences which deployment model fits well. A server that keeps nothing beyond the current request, no in memory cache tied to a specific instance, no session data held only in local variables, can be freely replicated, restarted, or moved between serverless invocations without anything breaking.

A server that quietly accumulates state in memory, an in process cache, a counter, a half finished multi step operation, works fine as a single process but becomes fragile the moment you add a second replica or let a serverless platform recycle instances underneath it. The Horizontal Scaling lesson later in this module goes deeper into exactly what statelessness requires in practice.
12. Cost Considerations Across Models

Cost follows a predictable shape across the three models. A single process on a fixed size machine costs the same whether it handles ten requests a day or ten thousand, which is efficient at steady moderate load and wasteful at very low load. Serverless flips this entirely, you pay per invocation and per millisecond of compute, which is efficient at low or spiky load and can become surprisingly expensive at sustained high volume.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model","Cost shape","Cheapest when"],"rows":[["Single process","Fixed, regardless of traffic","Traffic is steady and fills the capacity"],["Containerized","Scales with replica count","Traffic is predictable and moderate to high"],["Serverless","Scales with invocations","Traffic is low volume or highly bursty"]]}

blocks.text: 13. Deployment and Update Cadence

How often you expect to ship changes is worth factoring in early. A single process deployment usually means a manual or lightly scripted restart for every update, which is fine for infrequent changes but becomes a real bottleneck if you are shipping several times a day. Containerized deployments pair naturally with rolling updates, a new image version is rolled out replica by replica while old ones keep serving traffic, so users see no gap.

Serverless platforms typically make this even simpler at the platform level, a new version of your function is deployed and traffic shifts to it, often with built in support for gradually shifting a percentage of traffic to the new version before fully committing.
14. Security Boundaries Per Model

Each deployment model draws its isolation boundary in a different place. A single process shares the entire host machine with whatever else runs there, so a vulnerability in one dependency can, in the worst case, expose more than just your server. A container adds a real isolation boundary around the filesystem and process namespace, though it still shares the underlying kernel with other containers on the same host unless additional sandboxing is layered on.

Serverless platforms generally provide the strongest default isolation, since each invocation runs in an environment the platform itself manages and tears down, but that same opacity means you have less visibility into, and less control over, exactly how that isolation is implemented.

items: Single process: shares the full host, weakest default isolation, strongest operator visibility.
Containerized: isolates filesystem and process namespace, shares the kernel, moderate visibility.
Serverless: strongest platform managed isolation, least visibility into the underlying environment.

blocks.text: 15. Hybrid Deployment Patterns

blocks.alt: A hybrid pattern mixes container and serverless deployment for different parts

blocks.text: Real systems rarely commit to exactly one of these models for everything. It is common to run a core, steady traffic MCP server as a small containerized deployment while offloading a rarely used, spiky tool, a report generator invoked once a week, say, as a separate serverless function that shares the same underlying business logic.

items: A containerized primary server handling the bulk of steady tool calls.
A serverless function handling one infrequent, resource heavy tool.
A single process developer preview deployment used only during local testing.

blocks.text: The key is treating this as a per tool, or per workload, decision rather than assuming an entire MCP server must live under one single deployment model.
16. Migration Paths Between Models

Teams rarely pick the final deployment model on day one, and that is fine, the healthy pattern is starting with whichever model has the least operational overhead for your current traffic and migrating only once you have real evidence the current one is straining. Moving from a single process to a container is usually the smallest step, mostly a matter of writing a Dockerfile around code that barely changes.

Moving from containerized to serverless, or the reverse, asks more of your code, since it usually means adjusting how the server is invoked, one long lived process listening on a port versus a handler function invoked per request, so it helps to keep your core request handling logic decoupled from whichever entrypoint wraps it today.
17. A Decision Framework

blocks.alt: Traffic pattern and team size feed into choosing a deployment model

blocks.text: When none of the previous sections gives you an obvious answer, it helps to walk through a short, ordered set of questions rather than defaulting to whatever is trendy.

items: Is this server invoked over stdio by a single client process? If so, single process is effectively your only option.
Is traffic steady and predictable? Lean containerized with a fixed replica count.
Is traffic bursty, unpredictable, or very low volume? Lean serverless.
Does the server hold meaningful in memory state between requests? Rule out serverless until that state is externalized.
Do you ship changes multiple times a day? Favor whichever model gives you rolling or gradual updates.

blocks.text: 18. Rollback Strategies Across Models

blocks.alt: A bad deployment is rolled back to the previous known good version

blocks.text: However carefully you pick a deployment model, you will eventually ship a bad release, and how quickly you can undo it matters just as much as how carefully you rolled it out in the first place. A single process deployment usually rolls back by redeploying the previous binary or script and restarting, which works but typically means a brief gap in availability unless you script a blue green style swap yourself.

code.content:
# a simple rollback for a containerized deployment, reverting to the
# previously known good image tag
docker stop weather-mcp
docker run -d --name weather-mcp --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8080:8080 weather-mcp-server:1.3.0   # previous known-good tag

blocks.text: Containerized deployments make rollback almost mechanical, since every release is already an immutable, tagged image, reverting is just running the previous tag again. Serverless platforms usually go a step further and let you shift a percentage of traffic back to a previous version instantly, without a redeploy at all, which is one of the more underrated advantages of that model for teams that ship frequently.
Worked Example: Picking a Model for a Real Server

Consider a company internal MCP server that exposes tools for querying an internal knowledge base, used by roughly forty engineers through their coding assistants during business hours, with traffic dropping to near zero overnight and on weekends.
Walking the decision framework, the server is HTTP based, so all three models are technically available.
Traffic is bursty across the day rather than steady, which points away from a fixed size container deployment sized for peak hours that would sit mostly idle overnight.

code.content:
# a simple serverless-friendly handler wrapping the existing MCP logic
async def handler(event, context):
    mcp_request = parse_mcp_request(event["body"])
    result = await knowledge_base_server.handle(mcp_request)
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": serialize_mcp_response(result)}

blocks.text: The server holds no meaningful state between requests, each tool call independently queries the knowledge base and returns, so serverless is a clean fit here. The one adjustment worth making is enabling a small amount of provisioned concurrency during business hours to avoid cold starts hitting engineers first thing in the morning.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing a deployment model based on what is fashionable rather than actual traffic shape and team size.
Deploying a stateful server, one with in memory caches or counters, straight onto a serverless platform and being surprised when state disappears between invocations.
Running a single process deployment with no restart supervisor, so a crash means silent downtime until someone notices.
Trying to force a stdio based server behind a load balancer, which fundamentally misunderstands how stdio transport works.
Ignoring cold start latency until users start complaining about slow first requests after quiet periods.
Never revisiting the original deployment choice as traffic grows, and only discovering the mismatch during an incident.

blocks.text: Practice

Take an MCP server you have already written, or the lifecycle demo server from the previous lesson, and write out, in plain language, which of the three deployment models you would pick for three different scenarios: a personal side project only you use, a tool shared across a ten person team with steady daytime traffic, and a public facing tool with unpredictable spikes.

code.content:
# sketch out your reasoning for each scenario, for example:
# scenario: personal side project
# model: single process
# reasoning: one user, stdio transport, near zero operational overhead needed

blocks.text: For the public facing scenario, go one step further and sketch the serverless handler function signature you would wrap your existing tool logic in, paying attention to what state, if any, would need to move out of memory and into an external store first.
Key Takeaway

There is no universally correct MCP server deployment model, only a model that fits your transport, your traffic pattern, your statefulness, and your team's operational appetite better than the alternatives.

Single process deployment suits stdio servers and low traffic tools, containerized deployment suits steady, predictable HTTP traffic that benefits from orchestration, and serverless suits bursty or unpredictable traffic willing to trade occasional cold starts for near zero idle cost.

The next lesson, Dockerizing MCP Servers, picks up the containerized path in detail, walking through an actual Dockerfile for an MCP server and the specific considerations that change depending on whether that container speaks stdio or HTTP.
